Get Your Degree Online and Get a New Laptop

Get Your Degree Online and Get a New Laptop

by Olivia Mitchell | Sep 9, 2026

Updated: Oct 12, 2026

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:56
Instaread

Get your degree online, and get a new laptop out of the deal too. It sounds almost too convenient, but a growing number of colleges are bundling technology into their online programs, and if you’re already shopping for a degree, that’s a detail worth chasing down.

A Degree and the Machine to Earn It

Online programs exist because life doesn’t pause for class schedules. Adults juggling jobs, kids, and rent don’t need to relocate or clear out an evening commute; they need a laptop that won’t freeze during a proctored exam and a program that fits around everything else. That laptop isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s how you’ll watch lectures, message a professor at 11 p.m., submit a paper five minutes before the deadline, and, depending on your major, run software for accounting, coding, video editing, or design work that a five-year-old machine simply can’t handle.

Here’s the part nobody loves: buying that computer on top of tuition, textbooks, and application fees can turn “affordable online degree” into an unpleasant surprise. That’s exactly why some schools have started folding a laptop or a technology package into the cost of enrollment. Full Sail University, for instance, builds a customized technology package into its online tuition, tailored to whatever program a student is in. It won’t be the only school doing something like this, and it’s worth asking every admissions office you talk to whether they do too.

Not Every Laptop Program Works the Same Way

There’s no industry standard here, which is both good and annoying. Some colleges ship a laptop to every enrolled student and let them keep it outright. Others hand over the hardware early but attach strings: stay enrolled for a certain number of terms, or complete a minimum course load, and the laptop becomes yours. Drop out early, and you might owe the school a prorated cost or have to send the thing back in a padded envelope.

Then there are loaner programs, where the laptop never stops belonging to the college. You use it for the length of the program and return it at graduation, withdrawal, or even a semester-long break. It still solves the immediate problem of not owning a working computer, but you should know going in that it’s not building toward ownership.

A fourth option skips physical hardware handoffs altogether: a technology credit, scholarship, or bookstore allowance that a student can apply toward an approved laptop of their choosing. This tends to be more flexible since you’re not stuck with whatever model the school picked, though the allowance may not cover the full sticker price, so budget for a gap.

“Free” Is Doing a Lot of Work in That Sentence

Before you get too excited about a school advertising a free computer, read the fine print. In a lot of programs, the laptop’s cost is quietly folded into tuition or billed later as a technology fee. That doesn’t necessarily make it a bad deal, but it does mean the word “free” is doing some heavy lifting in the marketing copy, and you deserve the real math.

Call the admissions or financial aid office and ask directly: Is the laptop truly included at no extra charge, wrapped into tuition, purchasable through financial aid, or offered as a temporary loan? Will you own it the day it arrives, or only after hitting some enrollment milestone? And what happens if you drop a class, take a leave of absence, or transfer somewhere else, since a laptop that looked “free” on day one can turn into a bill the moment your enrollment status changes. It’s also smart to ask about warranties, accidental damage coverage, and who to call if the thing dies during finals week, because a dead laptop during an exam window is a genuinely bad time.

The Degree Still Comes First

A laptop is a nice perk. It is not a reason to enroll somewhere. Before you fall for a shiny technology package, figure out what you actually want the degree to do for you, whether that’s a promotion, a career pivot, or just getting back into the workforce after a few years away. Once you know the destination, you can start comparing programs that actually teach what employers in that field are asking for.

The Department of Education’s College Scorecard is a genuinely useful tool here, letting you compare completion rates, typical costs, and post-graduation outcomes across schools rather than relying on a glossy brochure. Running two or three programs through it side by side tends to reveal pretty quickly whether a laptop offer is attached to a serious academic program or just being used as bait. And don’t assume “online” means fully remote in every case. Some programs still require internships, lab hours, or the occasional trip to campus, which might be fine, but only if it actually fits your life.

Check Who’s Actually Accrediting the School

Accreditation sounds like paperwork until you need it, and then it matters enormously. An accredited school has been reviewed by an organization recognized by the relevant federal authorities, though accreditation alone doesn’t guarantee every single program is a great fit. You can look up any school through the Department of Education’s accreditation database rather than taking a college’s word for it, and honestly, it takes about two minutes.

If you’re heading into nursing, teaching, counseling, or another licensed field, programmatic accreditation matters just as much as the general kind. Ask the school directly whether the program satisfies licensing requirements in the state where you plan to actually work, because those rules vary and a degree that’s perfectly valid in one state can fall short in another. If you think you might transfer credits later or move on to a graduate program, check with those other schools now. They make the final call on what transfers, not the school you’re currently considering, no matter what the admissions rep promises.

Do the Full Math, Not Just the Sticker Price

A laptop might run you a few hundred dollars. Tuition differences between two comparable programs can run into the thousands, so keep your eye on the number that actually moves the needle. Add up tuition, mandatory fees, books, software subscriptions, and any technology charges that financial aid won’t touch, and ask point-blank whether tuition could rise while you’re still enrolled.

Then look at pacing. Accelerated formats can get you to graduation faster, but they demand a heavier weekly workload that isn’t realistic for everyone. A slower pace might be easier to balance with a full-time job and a family, even if it stretches out the total timeline and, sometimes, the total cost. There’s no universally “better” option here. The one that fits your actual schedule and budget is the right one, even if it’s not the fastest path on paper.

Don’t Skip the FAFSA

Plenty of online students qualify for the same federal aid available to their on-campus peers, provided the school is eligible and they meet the standard requirements. Filling out the FAFSA is the step that unlocks grants, loans, and work-study opportunities, and it’s worth submitting even if you’re fairly sure you won’t qualify for much, since your specific numbers might surprise you.

Once an offer comes back, separate the grants and scholarships from the loans. The first category generally doesn’t need to be repaid as long as you meet the conditions; the second does, plus interest, so treat those two piles of money very differently when deciding what to accept. It’s also worth asking the financial aid office whether a laptop can be factored into your cost of attendance. Policies differ by school and aren’t automatic, but there’s no harm in asking, and it beats taking out a bigger loan than necessary just to afford a premium machine when a mid-range one would do the job fine.

Making the Laptop Actually Earn Its Keep

Once you’re enrolled, the laptop can do more than open a portal and submit homework. Use it to build a portfolio of your best coursework, refresh your resume, run through mock interviews on video, and pick up whatever software is standard in your target field, assuming your school lets you keep and share your project files after the class ends. Students often forget that tutoring, academic advising, and career coaching are usually already baked into tuition, so it’s worth actually using those services instead of letting them sit unused for four years.

According to 2025 data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, workers aged 25 and older with more education tend to report higher median weekly earnings and lower unemployment than those with less. That’s a broad trend across large groups of people, not a promise about your specific paycheck, but it’s part of why so many adults keep circling back to the idea of finishing a degree later in life.

Where to Start

You don’t have to pick between waiting for the “right time” and actually doing something today. Start by shortlisting a few accredited programs that line up with your career goal, then run them through the Scorecard, check accreditation, and call each admissions office with a specific list of questions about cost, laptop policy, and what happens if your plans change mid-program. Get the laptop policy in writing before you commit to anything, because a verbal promise from an admissions call doesn’t hold up the way a signed agreement does.

The laptop is just a tool. The degree is what actually changes your options, so treat the technology perk as a bonus that sweetens a good decision rather than the reason you make one. If the timing feels right, there’s no real downside to spending an afternoon comparing two or three programs and finding out exactly what each one is offering, in writing, before you sign anything.
